chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 141-160: short speeches of kalavu and separation, most in the heroine's voice: night trysts refused and longed for (141, 150, 153), the lover's heart left behind (142, 156), the friend's comfort and the coming of marriage elders (143, 146, 159), the season and the dream that fail (147, 148, 155, 160), and three hens calling for absent mates (151, 154) beside the dawn, the storm and the elopement that part lovers (144, 157, 158).

141.reading: The heroine asks her friend what harm there would be in telling the lord of the slope that her mother has sent her to drive the curve-beaked parrots off the ripening millet, and in telling him not to come in the deep midnight, when a great tiger, bruised from a hard fight with an elephant, waits for its chance to kill a green-eyed red dog.
141.nuance: The mother's errand is reported as news, but it tells him where she will be by day, so 'do not come at night' is half of an offer. The beasts are reasons, not a mood: even the tiger on that slope is wounded and lying in wait to kill.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope and the dark midnight are kurinji's land and hour (porul 1.8)

142.reading: The hero wonders whether the simple girl with flower-like eyes, who threads a garland of pool flowers and drives the parrots off the millet field, knows or does not know that at midnight he breathes heavily like an elephant in its resting place and that his heart is still there beside her.
142.nuance: He has gone home but his heart has not, and he cannot tell whether she knows: the doubt of the first days of kalavu, before any word has passed between them. The sleeping elephant's breath gives the size of his longing in a scene of stillness.

thinai_evidence.note: pool flowers and the parrots of the millet field are kurinji things

comparisons.tenor: his heavy sighing at midnight, like the breathing of an elephant at rest

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; he speaks to himself

143.reading: The friend tells the heroine not to despair: the lord of the fruitful hill loves her greatly and fears blame, and since only impermanence is permanent, the pallor spread over her lovely skin cannot stay, any more than wealth stays with a dutiful man of kind heart who seeks good fame.
143.nuance: The maxim of impermanence, usually a warning, becomes comfort: what must pass includes her pallor. The simile is chosen with care, since the generous man's wealth leaves him because he gives it away: the pallor will leave by a good act, not by decay.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill country names the land of the lover

comparisons.tenor: the pallor on her body, which cannot stay, as wealth does not stay with a generous man

144.reading: The foster mother says it was good when the girl picked water-lilies in the backwater and played in the white-crested waves of the sea; she would not even stay here to play as she should with her inseparable friends, and has gone that way, over desolate gravel, to a mountain country of sky-high ridges where moving clouds crawl over the peaks.
144.nuance: She measures the going by landscapes: from the sea shore of the girl's play, across the stony waste, to the mountains beyond. பிரிவில் ஆயம், the troop that never parted from her, is the first thing she has parted from.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl's going over the gravel waste with her lover

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks of the girl

145.reading: The heroine says this little harbour village is no place to live: charging the lord of the seaside grove with cruelty, she suffers in unending sorrow at midnight, and the long night here holds only people with sleeping eyes, who will not talk with those who lie awake.
145.nuance: Who 'raises' the lord's cruelty is open, she or the village; either way the complaint lands on the sleepers, whose sleep is a refusal of company. Line 1's உறைபதி யன்றி may mean 'not our own town' rather than 'no place to dwell'.

thinai_evidence.note: the harbour village and the seaside grove are the shore

146.reading: The friend asks the heroine whether the people who unite the parted have come to their town: men with staffs in their hands and white cloths on their heads, who say 'good, good' and, there in their assembly, 'today is a great day'.
146.nuance: The elders are seen before their errand is named, by their staffs, white headgear and stock words of approval, so the friend lets the heroine read the signs of a marriage embassy herself and gives her joy as a question. வெண்டலை may be white heads of age rather than white cloth.

thinai_evidence.note: the coming of those who unite parted lovers turns kalavu toward marriage

147.reading: The hero tells the dream that, as if it had brought him the young woman of fine ornaments, whose lovely dark skin with its fine down is like the curved paathiri flower of summer, it wakes him from sweet sleep; those parted from their mates are not to be mocked.
147.nuance: He blames the dream, not waking: its gift is a trick that ends in waking, so its kindness is a kind of mockery. The last line widens his case into a rule for all the parted.

thinai_evidence.note: summer and the parted lover

comparisons.tenor: the fine down on her dark skin, like the curved paathiri flower of summer
the dream, acting as though it had brought her to him

148.reading: Answering a friend who says the season has not come, the heroine asks: if this great cool time, when konrai buds like the gold coins of the frog-mouthed anklets on rich children's small feet bloom along with the kurundham, is not the rainy season, then is this a dream?
148.nuance: The friend's usual argument, that the rains prove he will come, is turned round: the rains have come and he has not, so the friend must deny the season and the heroine must insist on it. Her question makes the comfort an admission that he broke his word.

thinai_evidence.note: konrai and kurundham in bloom mark the rains of the woodland

comparisons.tenor: the konrai buds, like the gold coins on the anklets of rich children

149.reading: The heroine says her modesty is to be pitied: it struggled long beside her, but now, like a small dam of heaped sand where white-flowered reeds grow, which gives way when the sweet flood presses, it has held as long as it could and, with desire pressing, no longer stays in her hand.
149.nuance: Modesty is a companion that 'suffered with us' and is pitied, not a law she breaks. The dam is small and of sand and the flood is sweet: the image concedes that what breaks it is welcome.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names no land; the colophon's paalai fits a restraint giving way before she goes with him

comparisons.vehicle: ஓங்குமணற் சிறுசிறை தீம்புனல் நெரிதர வீய்ந்துக் காஅங்கு
comparisons.tenor: her modesty, which held as long as it could and gives way as desire presses

150.reading: The heroine tells her friend that when she thinks of the sandal-dried chest of the lord of the high hill, where the fragrant smoking torches lit by the watchman on the platform flicker here and there like stars, the pain within her swells; when she embraces it, how is it that the pain vanishes?
150.nuance: Thought and embrace act on one sickness in opposite ways, and she asks why as if it were a riddle; the asking itself reports that the embrace has happened.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet watchman's torches on the high hill

comparisons.tenor: the watchman's smoking torches, flickering here and there like stars in the sky

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: அன்னாய், 'mother', is her address to the friend

151.reading: The hero says that, not counting it hard to take the narrow path through the hills where the red-legged hen, her mate felled by a hawk as he rose, cannot find him and keeps crying short flute-sweet calls, to leave behind the beloved he cannot forget and go: that is the end of youth.
151.nuance: 'Going is the end of youth' is a verdict, not a regret: youth is the time to be with her, and the road can wait. வங்காக் கடந்த in line 1 is hard; it may name the vangaa bird whose hen she is.

thinai_evidence.note: the question of leaving her for the road

comparisons.tenor: the hen's calls, sweet and sad as a flute

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he answers his own urge to leave

iraicchi.act: the hen, her mate struck down by a hawk as he rose, cannot find him and keeps calling
iraicchi.sense: a woman left behind would call so for a man lost on such roads, so the hero who hears it will not leave his beloved

152.reading: The heroine says those who reproach her know nothing at all: if her lover leaves it helpless, love, like the young of the tortoise, has nothing to do but lie within and waste away, as an egg does away from its mother.
152.nuance: The image rests on the old belief that the tortoise leaves her eggs in the sand and the young live by her thought of them: love too lives only by the lover's thought, and withdrawn it can only shrink where it lies. தாயின் in line 2 (with or without the mother) is the crux.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names no land; the friend's rebuke belongs to kalavu

comparisons.tenor: love lying hidden within and wasting, like an egg left by its mother
love left helpless by the lover, like the tortoise hatchling left by its mother

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: those who reproach her are the friend's words

153.reading: The heroine says her pitiable heart, which used to be afraid when the hill owl hooted or when the male monkey leapt on the dark branch of the jackfruit in the yard and shook it, now in the dense dark night never tires of going to him along the long way down the slope.
153.nuance: The old fears are household ones, an owl, a monkey in the yard; the journey the heart now makes is the lover's own night road. She speaks of the heart as a separate creature whose character has changed.

thinai_evidence.note: hill, slope and dark night

154.reading: The heroine asks her friend how they learned it, those who can part and live far away in the forest of the hard waste, where in the hour when heat shimmers like a snake's stretched slough the short-stepping hen with spotted neck feathers, thinking of the cock that went to find food, sits on the forked branch of the parched kalli and calls out in loneliness.
154.nuance: The cock has gone only to fetch food, the hero's own errand in small, and still the hen cries; 'how did they learn it' sets parting down as a skill learned against nature.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard waste in the hour of heat

comparisons.tenor: the shimmering heat of the hot hour, like a snake's sloughed skin stretched out

iraicchi.act: the hen, thinking of the cock gone to find food, sits on the kalli fork and calls in loneliness
iraicchi.sense: even a bird whose mate is only gone to fetch food cries out, so the man who knows that road knows what his going does to her

155.reading: The heroine says the hour has come when the farmers who cleared the old field with a great din bring their seed baskets brimming with flowers, but no word comes that his chariot is on its way, its clear split-mouthed bells, cast from wax moulds and poured in the furnace, ringing through the thick-treed thicket as it comes down from the waste to arrive in the evening for a great feast with guests.
155.nuance: The season and the hour are both here; what is missing is only the report, so she waits for news before the man. The chariot is drawn down to the casting of its bells, as if imagined over and over. விதைக்குறு வட்டி போதொடு பொதுள (line 2) is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the sowing time and the evening hour he named

156.reading: The hero calls to the Brahmin youth, who carries a water pot hung from a staff of red-flowered palasa stripped of its bark and eats the food of his vows: among the sweet words of your unwritten learning, is there a medicine with the power to unite those who are parted, or is this madness?
156.nuance: எழுதாக் கற்பு, the learning not written, names the Veda by how it is kept, by mouth. மயலோ இதுவே leaves it open whether the madness is the question or the hero's own state, and so whether he mocks the Brahmin's lore or truly hopes in it.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero in kalavu asks for the means of union

157.reading: The heroine says that when the cock cried 'kukkoo' her pure heart started in fear, for dawn had come like a sword that cuts apart lovers whose shoulders touch.
157.nuance: The cock is only the signal; the sword is the dawn itself. Her heart is pure and still it starts as at a blow, as if dawn's cut fell on her.

thinai_evidence.note: the cock and dawn are marutham's hour (porul 1.9)

comparisons.tenor: dawn, which cuts apart lovers whose shoulders touch, like a sword

158.reading: The heroine asks the dark cloud heavy with rain, which came on the wind mingled with the roar of the swift thunder that strikes snakes dead on the slopes of the tall mountain, whether it has no pity: it has power to shake even the famed Himalaya, so what is this against women who are pitiable for want of a companion?
158.nuance: The storm's might is granted and then turned into a reproach: a power that can shake the Himalaya has no need to try itself on a lone woman. The strong thing that leaves her unprotected stands for the absent man.

thinai_evidence.note: the tall mountain in the storm of night

159.reading: The friend says that the girl's slender waist, too small to bear the leaf skirt on her hips, is in distress, for her soft chest has filled out and her round streaked breasts have risen to rival caskets, while this foolish town, full of worry, keeps saying with sorrowful hearts 'what will become of her, the girl with flower earrings?' and consults no one.
159.nuance: Her coming of age is told as a burden on her waist and as worry in the town; both mean she will now be watched and kept at home, so said in the lover's hearing it presses him to marry. உசாவா in line 6 may mean the town will not consult her family, or will not talk to her.

thinai_evidence.note: the leaf skirt of the hill girl

comparisons.tenor: her breasts, risen to rival caskets

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is inferred from the matter: the girl's coming of age told in the lover's hearing

160.reading: The heroine tells her friend that at hushed midnight, when the fire-red-headed anril cries with its prawn-beaked hen from their nest on the tall branch, making the parted helpless, and the great cold north wind blows as well, he does not come: so this is our lover's coming!
160.nuance: The last line is bitter irony: the cries and the wind are all that came. The anril pair in one nest is the measure of her single bed.

thinai_evidence.note: midnight is kurinji's hour (porul 1.8) and the cold north wind its season

comparisons.tenor: the anril's red head, like fire
the hen's curved beak, like a prawn

iraicchi.act: the anril keeps with its hen in their nest on the tall branch through the cold midnight and cries
iraicchi.sense: even the birds keep their mates through the cold night, while her lover, who said he would come, stays away

links.note: Akananuru 18 has the same thurai, the night-comer told to come by day: the friend tells the hill lord the night ford is deadly and he may meet the girl by day in the kaanthal grove. Kuruntokai 141 gives the refusal to the heroine, who only reports her mother's errand to the millet field.
links.teaches: Held together they show the one message in two voices: the friend may name the day meeting outright, while the heroine can offer it only by passing on her mother's errand, so the day tryst comes through indirection exactly where the speaker's freedom is narrowest.

links.note: Naladiyar 2: wealth stays level with no one but turns like a cart wheel, so share it the day it comes. Kuruntokai 143 uses the wealth that does not stay with a generous man as the image of pallor that will pass.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar argues from wealth's instability to giving, and the love poem had already fused the two into one image, the giver whose wealth leaves him, and turned that ethical commonplace into a promise that sorrow too is the kind of thing that leaves.

links.note: Kural 331 calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for lasting. Kuruntokai 143's friend says impermanence alone is permanent, and draws hope from it.
links.teaches: The Kural uses impermanence to rebuke attachment, but the friend of the love poem applies the same truth to grief, showing that the doctrine was a two-edged tool: what cannot last includes the pallor of longing, so it consoles as readily as it warns.

links.note: Kural 1168: the night that puts all living things to sleep is pitiable, having no companion but her. Kuruntokai 145: the long night here has only sleepers who will not talk with the sleepless.
links.teaches: Both women stay awake while everyone sleeps, but the Kural turns her loneliness into a mock pity for the night, while the Kuruntokai blames the sleeping village; together they show that the wakeful heroine's complaint can fall on the night or on the people, and that the couplet's wit grows from the poem's social grievance.

links.note: 146: the friend asks whether 'those who unite the parted' (பிரிந்தோர்ப் புணர்ப்போர்) have come, staffs in hand. 156: the hero asks the Brahmin with his staff whether his learning holds a medicine 'that unites the parted' (பிரிந்தோர்ப் புணர்க்கும்).
links.teaches: The same phrase names the go-between's office from both sides of kalavu: in the friend's mouth the uniters arrive as joyful elders of a marriage embassy, while the hero doubts that a Brahmin's book can unite anyone, so the phrase shows that union was expected from social go-betweens, not from learning.

links.note: Kural 1216: if there were no waking, the lover met in the dream would not leave. Kuruntokai 147: the hero says the dream, as if it had brought her, rouses him from sweet sleep.
links.teaches: The Kural's woman blames waking and spares the dream; the Kuruntokai's man blames the dream itself for ending his sleep, so set together they show that the dream meeting was felt as both gift and cheat, and that the blame shifts with which side of it the lover dwells on.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend shows the bloomed konrai and the dancing peacocks and calls the season medicine for the pallor. Kuruntokai 148: the friend denies that the konrai and kurundham mean the rains, and the heroine asks if she is dreaming.
links.teaches: The friend's proof from the season only works before the season is spent; once the konrai has bloomed and he has not come, the same flower proves his breach, so the comforter must deny the season and the heroine turns the argument against her.

links.note: Kural 1134: the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness (the man speaks). Kuruntokai 149: her modesty is a small sand dam that holds as long as it can and gives way when the sweet flood presses (the woman speaks).
links.teaches: Both picture desire as a flood against shame, but for the man shame is a raft that is swept away with him on it, and for the woman it is a dam that holds the water back, so the shared image is divided by gender: his shame rides the flood, hers resists it.

links.note: Kural 1251: the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted by shame (the woman speaks). Kuruntokai 149: her modesty struggled long, held as long as it could and now gives way.
links.teaches: The Kural states the collapse of restraint as a single blow of an axe, while the Kuruntokai gives it duration and fellowship, a modesty that 'suffered with us' long before giving way, which shows the couplet compressing a process the older poem tells as a struggle.

links.note: Kural 1104: the man asks where she got this fire that burns when he moves away and cools when he draws near. Kuruntokai 150: the woman says the pain swells when she thinks of his chest and vanishes when she embraces it.
links.teaches: The Kural's man finds the paradoxical fire in the woman, but the Kuruntokai heroine finds the same sickness in herself and sets it off by memory, not distance, so the pair shows that the burning-and-cooling belongs to both lovers and that thinking of the absent one is itself the burning.

links.note: 151: on the hill path a hen whose mate fell to a hawk keeps calling, and the hero decides leaving her would be the end of youth. 154: in the waste a hen whose cock has gone to find food calls in loneliness, and the heroine asks how men learn to part.
links.teaches: The same carrier, a hen calling for an absent mate on the road, works from both sides of the separation: in the hero's mouth it is the reason he stays, in the heroine's it is the reproach to a man who went anyway, so one native image can hold both the decision and its blame.

links.note: Akananuru 337: the hero reminds his heart, which presses for another journey, that once it found parting no joy, said 'let wealth stay where it is' and came back alone through the robbers' waste. Kuruntokai 151: the hero refuses the hill path, saying going would end his youth.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai 151 gives the moment of refusal, and Akananuru 337 shows that such a refusal does not settle anything: the heart that once turned back is urging the road again, so the decision not to leave is a choice that must be remade, not a resolution.

links.note: 141: the heroine asks the friend to tell the lover not to come in the deep night, when the tiger lies in wait on the slope. 153: her heart, once afraid of an owl or a monkey in the yard, now goes along the slope to him in the dense dark night.
links.teaches: The dangers of the night slope are the argument she uses to keep him away, yet her own heart travels that road without fear, so the pairing shows the night-danger plea as care for him rather than prudence she lives by.

links.note: Kural 1249: the woman asks her heart where it goes seeking, since the lover lives within it. Kuruntokai 153: her heart, once timid, now goes along the night slope to him without tiring.
links.teaches: The Kural mocks the heart's going out as needless because he is already within, while the Kuruntokai heroine marvels at the same going as courage, so the pairing shows the couplet's wit resting on an older picture of the heart as a traveller on the lover's road.

links.note: Kuruntokai 156: the lovesick hero asks the Brahmin whether his unwritten learning holds a medicine to unite the parted. Kural 1102: the man says other illnesses have other cures, but this woman is herself the cure for her sickness.
links.teaches: The couplet reads as the answer to the Kuruntokai hero's question: no learned remedy exists, because only the woman herself cures the sickness she causes, so the pair turns the hero's doubt of the Brahmin's lore into the Kural's general rule of love's medicine.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 10: as thunder roars and the bull bellows back, the swift chariot comes with the sound of a forest stream. Kuruntokai 155: the evening of the season has come, but not the word that his chariot with its ringing bells is on its way.
links.teaches: The venba lets the sound of the chariot arrive with the season, but the Kuruntokai keeps season and chariot apart and has the heroine wait first for the report of it, which shows the chariot-sound of mullai as a promise the older poem could leave unkept.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 17: on the high rock-ledged hill the thunder crushes snakes and the sky, thick with dark, shows the season; the friend reads it as his return. Kuruntokai 158: the heroine asks the cloud, whose thunder strikes snakes dead on the tall slope, whether it has no pity on lone women.
links.teaches: The same storm with its snake-killing thunder is a sign of comfort when the friend reads it as the promised season and a terror when the lone heroine faces it at night, so the image carries whatever the speaker's situation gives it rather than a fixed meaning.

links.note: Akananuru 305: on cold north-wind midnights a single anril on the palm cries in grief, and the heroine asks how she can live while he is away for wealth. Kuruntokai 160: at hushed midnight in the cold north wind the anril cries with its hen from their nest, and he does not come.
links.teaches: The anril's midnight cry in the north wind is shared, but the Akananuru bird is alone and mirrors her, while the Kuruntokai bird is with its mate and shows what she lacks; together they show that the anril, bird of the unparted, can serve as either likeness or contrast to the waiting woman.

links.note: Akananuru 17: the foster mother remembers how the girl, tired after ball and jacks, would lie in her arms, and wonders how her small feet will manage the waste. Kuruntokai 144: the foster mother remembers the girl's play in the backwater and the waves and sees her gone over the gravel to the far mountains.
links.teaches: Both foster mothers measure the elopement by the girl's play, but the Akananuru measures it on the body (tired feet, sweat), while the Kuruntokai measures it on the map, from sea shore through waste to mountain, so the pair shows the sevili's lament working through both the body and the landscapes the girl crosses.
